title: Cracking down on shadow AI is making your business less secure, not more
excerpt: Why banning shadow AI increases organizational security risks
content_html:
Security is always a moving target. But AI has made it move faster than many organizations can manage, presenting a gargantuan challenge for SOC teams. The near constant stream of announcements of new models or providers has resulted in a massively expanded attack surface.

Senior Product Manager at Nexthink.

While security teams work hard to review and approve as many tools as possible, the volume is still crushingly high. Today, only 22% of workers rely exclusively on the AI tools their employer provides, while more than a third (35%) of Gen Z employees say they prefer using personal AI applications over company-approved ones. For every sanctioned tool a business governs, most of its workforce is quietly working around it.

If almost 80% of employees use unapproved AI tools, then it isn’t an aberration - it’s the default. Shadow AI is normal across organizations, but the scale of the challenge is badly underestimated by the people responsible for managing it.

Why the crackdown backfires

Faced with unsanctioned use, the instinct is to clamp down. Blacklist as many tools as possible and pull usage back inside the lines. The problem is that, while this feels like control, in reality it just leaves security blind.

Blocking doesn’t stop an employee using a tool, it just drives the risk out of sight. If their tool of choice is blocked on their laptop, they’ll access it on their phone. Or with their personal email address instead of their work one.

This is true of many IT tools, but especially so with AI because people can become extremely attached to specific chatbot personalities. Consequently, AI use is driven deeper into the shadows, leaving zero visibility or record for security teams about potential data leakages or other risks.

This is the trap at the center of most shadow AI strategies. The harder an organization tries to eliminate the problem, the less it can see. And the less it can see, the more dangerous the problem becomes. Governance that looks airtight on paper can bear little resemblance to what’s actually happening across the business.

The consequences are not abstract. When confidential information flows into unmanaged third-party platforms, the fallout can add as much as $670,000 to the cost of a data breach, and most of the employees responsible have no idea they’ve created a risk at all.

Policy isn’t enforcement

The reason for these problems comes back to the speed at which AI development is moving. ChatGPT is barely five years old and the difference in performance over that time is immense. One result of this is that pretty much any AI security and best practice training employees have done has not been adequate.

The idea was not to overload employees with too much information. By keeping it ultra-straightforward and focusing on only one or two tools that were security-approved with examples looking at low-risk, early-adoption scenarios, companies could make compliance as easy possible.

For a normal technology, it would be a sensible strategy. However, the level of self-driven AI adoption we’ve seen has been far higher than companies expected. Shadow AI use is rampant and so security cannot afford to continue blindly enforcing rules that aren’t working.

Rather, to govern employee behavior, you need to be able to understand and analyze it. When it comes to AI that means gaining visibility into what tools and models employees are using, how, and where it’s actually delivering value.

An experience-based approach

That shift requires visibility into how AI is used across the workforce. A DEX (Digital Employee Experience) approach delivers exactly that, automatically detecting both approved and shadow AI through traffic patterns and endpoint activity, without relying on employees to self-report.

Usage and experience data sit in a single view, broken down by team and workflow, so leaders can see where people are working around the rules and act on it.

From there, the response stops being a blunt ban and becomes far more useful. In-app guidance can steer employees towards sanctioned tools in the flow of work, reinforcing the right behavior without killing the productivity they were chasing in the first place.

Policies can be built around real usage instead of guesswork. And because 96% of leaders now say digital adoption support is critical to AI readiness, that same visibility shows exactly where training will close a gap rather than tick a box.

It’s time to manage shadow AI

Shadow AI isn't going anywhere, and pretending otherwise is how organizations end up exposed. The companies that handle it well will be the ones that stop trying to ban it and start paying attention to it. Everyone else is just hoping their policy is being followed, with no real way of knowing whether it is.

面对未经批准的使用，人们的本能反应是予以制止。 将尽可能多的工具列入黑名单，并将使用量拉回线路内。 问题在于，虽然这感觉像是控制，但实际上它只会让安全性变得盲目。

阻止并不能阻止员工使用工具，它只是让风险消失。 如果他们选择的工具在笔记本电脑上被阻止，他们将在手机上访问它。 或者使用他们的个人电子邮件地址而不是他们的工作电子邮件地址。

许多 IT 工具都是如此，尤其是人工智能，因为人们可能会对特定的聊天机器人个性极度依恋。 因此，人工智能的使用被推向更深的阴影，使安全团队对潜在数据泄漏或其他风险的可见性或记录为零。

这是大多数影子人工智能策略的核心陷阱。 组织越努力消除问题，看到的就越少。 它能看到的越少，问题就变得越危险。 纸面上看起来无懈可击的治理与整个企业实际发生的情况几乎没有相似之处。

其后果并不抽象。 当机密信息流入不受管理的第三方平台时，数据泄露的后果可能会增加高达 670,000 美元，而且大多数负责的员工根本不知道他们已经造成了风险。

政策不是执行

这些问题的根源在于人工智能发展的速度。 ChatGPT 才诞生了不到五年，而这段时间的性能差异是巨大的。 其结果之一是，员工所做的几乎所有人工智能安全和最佳实践培训都是不够的。

我们的想法是不要让员工承受过多的信息。 通过保持超简单并仅关注一两个经过安全批准的工具以及针对低风险、早期采用场景的示例，公司可以使合规性变得尽可能容易。

对于普通技术来说，这将是一个明智的策略。 然而，我们所看到的自我驱动人工智能的采用水平远远高于公司的预期。 影子人工智能的使用非常猖獗，因此安全部门不能继续盲目执行不起作用的规则。

相反，为了管理员工的行为，您需要能够理解和分析它。 谈到人工智能，这意味着要了解员工正在使用哪些工具和模型、如何以及在何处实际交付价值。

基于经验的方法

这种转变需要了解人工智能在整个劳动力中的使用方式。 DEX（数字员工体验）方法正是实现了这一点，通过流量模式和端点活动自动检测批准的人工智能和影子人工智能，而无需依赖员工自我报告。

使用情况和体验数据位于一个视图中，按团队和工作流程细分，因此领导者可以看到人们在哪些方面围绕规则工作并采取行动。

从那时起，回应就不再是生硬的禁令，而是变得更加有用。 应用内指导可以引导员工在工作流程中使用认可的工具，强化正确的行为，而不会破坏他们最初追求的生产力。

策略可以围绕实际使用而不是猜测来制定。 而且，由于 96% 的领导者现在表示数字化采用支持对于人工智能准备就绪至关重要，因此同样的可见性准确地显示了培训将在哪些方面缩小差距，而不是勾选框。

是时候管理影子人工智能了

影子人工智能不会消失，假装不这样做才是组织最终暴露的方式。 处理得好的公司将停止试图禁止它并开始关注它。 其他人都只是希望他们的政策得到遵守，但没有真正的方法知道它是否得到遵守。
